messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 59
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Professor
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Stress: Stress
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame had been a professor for most of his adult life, a man used to speaking calmly in lecture halls and offices, but the event that brought him to treatment had nothing to do with his work and everything to do with his younger sister. More than a year earlier, during a heavy storm season, she had been driving home when floodwater rose quickly across a low stretch of road. He had received the call from a nephew frantic and breathless, saying the car had been found near a bridge and that rescuers were searching the water. Kwame spent that night at the edge of the river with his family, smelling mud, gasoline, and stagnant water, watching headlights sweep across a floodplain that seemed to swallow sound. His sister was later recovered alive, but the memory of that night remained fixed in his mind with the smell of water and the sight of moving floodwater under harsh lights. Since then, water, flooding, and even large bodies of water had become potent reminders of what had happened, especially when he encountered them unexpectedly around campus, near drainage channels after rain, or on his drive home past the harbor. Related smells could seize him just as powerfully, carrying him back to that night in an instant.

What troubled Kwame most was how quickly his body now responded before he could think. When a storm passed and runoff collected in the quad outside his office, or when he caught a damp, riverlike smell in a hallway after cleaning, his chest tightened and his muscles braced as if something were about to happen again. He described it as his body reacting to danger before his mind had time to catch up, a jolt that would come before any clear thought and leave him feeling exposed and unsettled. In those moments he was flooded not only with fear but with horror and a sharp, lingering shame that he had been powerless to protect his sister. He would tell himself, even while sitting safely at his desk, that he should be able to calm down, yet he found he could not relax in a safe place once those sensations had started. The physical alarm felt convincing to him; because his body responded so strongly, he became more watchful for anything that might set it off again.

Over time, that expectation of alarm made the world feel narrower. Kwame found himself scanning weather reports before leaving for work and choosing routes that avoided roads near water. On campus, he became uneasy when rain pooled around the science building or when maintenance sprayed down walkways, and he noticed his attention snagging on the odor of wet concrete after storms. At first he tried to push through, but each encounter seemed to confirm how vulnerable he still felt, and the sense of threat intensified rather than eased. The more he noticed his body tense at the sight or smell of water, the more he trusted those signals, and the more he anticipated that danger might arrive again without warning. He began sitting through lectures with a portion of his mind on alert, monitoring his breathing and the tightness in his chest instead of fully engaging with his students. Even in his apartment, where nothing was objectively wrong, he remained unable to settle, as if some part of him were waiting for the next cue.

As the months passed, Kwame’s avoidance became part of his routine. He stopped taking evening walks by the riverfront he had once enjoyed, declined invitations that involved boating or waterfront restaurants, and rearranged errands so he would not have to pass the reservoir near his neighborhood. When rain was forecast, he would work from home if possible, telling colleagues only that the weather made commuting difficult. Those choices brought temporary relief, but they also kept him distant from ordinary life and increasingly aware of how many places now felt risky. He began to feel embarrassed by the extent of his reactions, especially because he had always seen himself as composed and in control. The shame made it harder to talk about what had happened, so he remained largely silent with friends and family, even as his sister urged him to stop carrying it alone. The silence left him alone with the same warning system that had been set off at the floodbank, and the alarm seemed to come faster each time he met a reminder.

By the time he sought help, Kwame was exhausted by the constant vigilance and by the way his professor’s life had shrunk around weather, smells, and sudden surges of stress. A tense week of heavy rain on campus finally pushed him to make an appointment after he found himself gripping the edge of his desk during a lecture, heart racing at the smell of damp carpeting drifting in from the corridor. He came because he was tired of feeling that his body had its own mind and because he feared one more reminder would leave him unable to work or be present for the people who still mattered to him. What he most hoped for was simple: to be able to stand in a safe place again without waiting for his body to sound the alarm.
